idiom_name: iterator method with yield return + Enumerable.Where/Select/Take
implementation_notes: C# realizes the lazy collection as IEnumerable<T>: an iterator method with yield return hands back one element per MoveNext and resumes where it left off, and the LINQ standard query operators are deferred - the query object is built immediately but runs only when the sequence is enumerated, which the documentation states as 'evaluation is delayed until its realized value is actually required'. The operators re-run the source per enumeration (no memoization), so cache with System.Lazy<T>/ToList when elements are expensive; hand-written enumerators remain justified for custom lifetime or for streaming sources that need disposal.
pitfalls: A LINQ query is deferred, not memoized: enumerating it twice re-runs the source (and its side effects), so a query over an expensive or non-deterministic source must be materialized.
Exceptions thrown inside an iterator surface at MoveNext on the consumer's thread and stack, far from the calling method that created the query.
Resource cleanup in an iterator only runs if the enumerator is disposed - foreach does it, but manual GetEnumerator()/MoveNext() loops that break early must use using/Dispose.

variants.name: IAsyncEnumerable<T> async streams (C# 8)
variants.idiom_name: async IAsyncEnumerable<T> with await foreach / await yield
variants.implementation_notes: When each element depends on awaited work - paged HTTP calls, database reads, queue consumption - C# 8's async streams express the same deferred pull model asynchronously: an async iterator method yields elements, await foreach pulls them with backpressure, and cancellation flows through [EnumeratorCancellation]/WithCancellation. It replaces the blocking IEnumerable pipeline rather than composing with it; the synchronous variant remains simpler when nothing is awaited and the elements are cheap.
pitfalls: An async iterator cannot be enumerated twice and is tied to the caller's token; combining WithCancellation with a token used elsewhere can silently change behaviour.
Forgetting [EnumeratorCancellation] makes the cancellation token a parameter value only, so the iterator keeps running after the caller cancels.
Async streams are not System.Linq-compatible without System.Linq.Async, so mixing them with IEnumerable LINQ operators forces eager buffering.
